extracted.intended_audience: learned Christian readers, clergy, and theologians evaluating worship/practice
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and apply standards for what counts as worship, idolatry, images, and related church practices (e.g., processions, canonization, exorcism), based on scriptural and natural-reason arguments in the treatise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Worship
rubrics_metrics.description: To Pray to, to Swear by, to Obey, to be Diligent, and Officious in Serving: in summe, all words and actions that betoken Fear to Offend, or Desire to Please, is Worship (Lat. cultus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worship is primarily inward honor expressed by outward signs; any external acts that signify esteem or service count as worship, whether sincere or feigned. Use this to identify acts that qualify as worship rather than mere custom or civility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Divine and Civill Worship
rubrics_metrics.description: The Worship we exhibite to those we esteem to be but men ... is Civill Worship: But the worship we exhibite to that which we think to bee God ... is Divine Worship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the worshipper's belief and the object of veneration: acts done to honor a mortal authority (even prostration) are civil worship unless the worshipper treats the object as God. The terms douleia and latreia are used interchangeably in Scripture; intention and relation to sovereign power matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: When external compulsion is not idolatry
rubrics_metrics.description: If a King compell a man to it by the terrour of Death, or other great corporall punishment, it is not Idolatry: ... which is not a sign that he that obeyeth him, does inwardly honour him as a God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an individual performs outward worship under coercion and does not inwardly honor the image/sovereign, this outward act is not to be judged as idolatry; but consider whether the person is a public example (see scandalous worship).

rubrics_metrics.name: Idolatry defined (worship of Images)
rubrics_metrics.description: To worship an Image, is voluntarily to doe those externall acts, which are signes of honoring either the matter of the Image ... or the Phantasme of the brain ... or both together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify as idolatry when external acts signify genuine internal honor or belief that the image (matter or represented phantasm) has divine power or hears prayers. Distinguish from mere memorial or civil honor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scandalous Worship (seeming worship by pastors/authorities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scandalous Worship ... is but Seeming Worship; and may sometimes bee joined with an inward, and hearty detestation ... and proceed onely from the fear of death, or other grievous punishment; and is neverthelesse a sin in them that so worship, in case they be men whose actions are looked at by others, as lights to guide them by.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When persons of public authority outwardly perform worship they detest, they create scandal and lead others astray; this is sinful for those with pastoral/public influence even if inwardly they reject the practice. Evaluate both the actor's status and the effect on others' consciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissibility of images appointed by God
rubrics_metrics.description: The places of Scripture pretended to countenance the setting up of Images ... As for the proofs alledged out of Scripture, namely, those examples of Images appointed by God to bee set up; They were not set up for the people, or any man to worship; but that they should worship God himselfe before them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Images or representations expressly commanded or instituted by God (e.g., cherubim over the ark, brazen serpent) are not idolatrous when used to worship God; such cases require explicit divine warrant or authoritative scriptural sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Images as memorials or civil honors (non-idolatrous uses)
rubrics_metrics.description: I say not, that to draw a Picture after a fancy, is a Sin; ... for such use of an Image, is not Worship of the Image; but a civill honoring of the Person, not that is, but that was.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between using images as monuments, memorials, or civil commemorations (permissible) versus treating them as objects of divine power (idolatrous). Evaluate the intention and public presentation of the image.

rubrics_metrics.name: No image of the invisible or infinite
rubrics_metrics.description: It is also evident, that there can be no Image of a thing Infinite: for all the Images ... are figured ... And therefore there can bee no Image of God: nor of the Soule of Man; nor of Spirits, but onely of Bodies Visible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theologically, representations cannot capture God or infinite substances; any claim that an image literally represents or contains God or spirits is inherently mistaken and tends toward idolatry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Painting visions or fancies is not sinful; worshipping them is
rubrics_metrics.description: I say not, that to draw a Picture after a fancy, is a Sin; but when it is drawn, to hold it for a Representation of God, is against the second Commandement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artistic depiction of dreams, visions, or imagined angels is permissible as long as the depiction is not treated as a literal representation of God or a saint who can hear prayers; evaluate subsequent uses and attributions given to such images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worship directed to images for reasons reserved to God is idolatry
rubrics_metrics.description: To pray to a King for such things, as hee is able to doe for us, though we prostrate our selves before him, is but Civill Worship; But voluntarily to pray unto him for fair weather, or for any thing which God onely can doe for us, is Divine Worship, and Idolatry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If worship/prayer directed to an image or creature seeks divine actions (miracles, control of nature) that only God can perform, classify it as idolatry. Distinguish pragmatic petitions to humans from petitions that attribute divine power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of scriptural language about spirits and possession
rubrics_metrics.description: I find in Scripture that there be Angels, and Spirits, good and evill; but not that they are Incorporeall, as are the Apparitions men see in the Dark, or in a Dream, or Vision ... And I find that there are Spirits Corporeal, (though subtile and Invisible;) but not that any mans body was possessed, or inhabited by them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing claims of demonic possession or exorcism, consider natural explanations (disease, frenzy, visions) and the textual usage of 'spirit' as sometimes referring to inner dispositions; be cautious in treating every report as literal incorporeal possession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraordinary gifts in primitive church were temporary
rubrics_metrics.description: it is probable, that those extraordinary gifts were given to the Church, for no longer a time, than men trusted wholly to Christ ... and consequently, that when they sought Authority, and Riches ... these supernaturall gifts of God were again taken from them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate contemporary claims of miraculous or extraordinary spiritual gifts against historical context: such gifts may have been temporary signs for the early church and are not automatic endorsements of current similar claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adoption of pagan rites without warrant is a relic of Gentilisme
rubrics_metrics.description: Another relike of Gentilisme, is the Worship of Images ... The cause whereof, was the immoderate esteem, and prices set upon the workmanship of them ... And as worldly ambition creeping by degrees into the Pastors, drew them to an endeavour of pleasing the new made Christians ... so the worshipping of the Images of Christ and his Apostles, grow more and more Idolatrous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat adoption of external rites (processions, candled torches, holy water, wakes, carnivals) derived from pagan customs with suspicion unless there is scriptural or legitimate ecclesiastical sanction; evaluate origin and function of ritual elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonization requires proper authority; unchecked canonizing is pagan relic
rubrics_metrics.description: The Canonizing of Saints, is another Relique of Gentilisme: It is neither a misunderstanding of Scripture, nor a new invention of the Roman Church, but a custome as ancient as the Common-wealth of Rome it self.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess claims of saintly status by whether there is legitimate, authoritative warrant rather than popular anecdote; cataloging posthumous sainthood without authoritative process resembles apotheosis and pagan practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Processions and ceremonial pomp as derived practices (evaluate origin and meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: The carrying about of Images in Procession, is another Relique of the Religion of the Greeks, and Romans ... And that which they called Pompa, is the same that now is named Procession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating processions, ceremonial pomp, or public honors (candles, shrines, carrying of images), examine whether they serve to honor God rightly or perpetuate pagan forms; determine whether practice has ecclesiastical sanction and avoids encouraging idolatrous belief among the ignorant.
